revealWordProblem.title: Apply: Party Plans
revealWordProblem.text: Reginald is having hot dogs at his party, and 24 people are coming. His mom wants the same number of hot dogs and buns, with none left over. Hot dogs come in packs of 10 and buns come in packs of 8. How many packs of each should they buy, and how many hot dogs and buns will they have?
revealWordProblem.sampleAnswer: Nothing is being split into groups here — packs are being counted forward until the two totals match — so this is a least-common-multiple problem. Multiples of 10: 10, 20, 30, 40 …. Multiples of 8: 8, 16, 24, 32, 40 …. The first total both pack sizes reach exactly is 40, so the LCM of 10 and 8 is 40. That means 4 packs of hot dogs (4 × 10 = 40) and 5 packs of buns (5 × 8 = 40), giving 40 of each with none left over — more than enough for 24 guests. Any smaller number of packs would leave some hot dogs without buns.

vocabulary.definition: Listing what divides a number evenly (its factors) and what it divides into evenly (its multiples), then finding what two numbers share.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Listar lo que divide un número exactamente (sus factores) y lo que el número forma al contar de esa cantidad (sus múltiplos), y luego hallar lo que dos números comparten.
vocabulary.visual: GCF of 48 and 36 is 12 · LCM of 6 and 8 is 24

vocabulary.definition: A whole number that divides another number evenly, with no remainder.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Un número entero que divide a otro exactamente, sin residuo.

vocabulary.definition: The result of multiplying a number by 1, 2, 3, and so on — where you land when you skip-count by it.
vocabulary.definitionEs: El resultado de multiplicar un número por 1, 2, 3, y así sucesivamente: donde caes al contar de esa cantidad.

vocabulary.definition: The largest number that is a factor of two or more numbers. It answers “how many equal groups can I make?”
vocabulary.definitionEs: El número más grande que es factor de dos o más números. Responde “¿cuántos grupos iguales puedo formar?”

vocabulary.definition: The smallest number that is a multiple of two or more numbers. It answers “when will these line up again?”
vocabulary.definitionEs: El número más pequeño que es múltiplo de dos o más números. Responde “¿cuándo volverán a coincidir?”

vocabulary.definition: Two factors that multiply to make a number. In a word problem, one is the number of groups and the other is the size of each group.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Dos factores que se multiplican para formar un número. En un problema, uno es la cantidad de grupos y el otro el tamaño de cada grupo.

vocabulary.definition: Writing a number as a product of prime numbers, usually with a factor tree. Multiplying the primes two numbers share also gives the GCF.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Escribir un número como producto de números primos, normalmente con un árbol de factores. Multiplicar los primos que dos números comparten también da el MCD.

conceptIntro.heading: Factors split things up; multiples count forward
conceptIntro.intro: A factor divides a number evenly, so factors answer questions about splitting a stock into equal groups. A multiple is where you land when you skip-count, so multiples answer questions about when repeating events line up.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: GCF = the biggest number that divides BOTH — use it to split into equal groups. LCM = the smallest number BOTH divide into — use it to find when cycles meet again.

iDo.title: Watch me build the combo packs
lines: The store has 48 pencils and 36 notebooks. Every combo pack must hold the same number of each, with nothing left over — so the number of packs has to be a factor of BOTH quantities.
Factors of 48: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 24, 48. Factors of 36: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36. Listing them in order is what makes the comparison easy.
The numbers in both lists are the common factors: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, and 12.
The greatest of those is 12, so the GCF of 48 and 36 is 12. The manager can make 12 combo packs — each holding 48 ÷ 12 = 4 pencils and 36 ÷ 12 = 3 notebooks.

weDo.title: Let's do one together — the same GCF, using prime factors
lines: A factor tree breaks each number into primes. 48 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 3, and 36 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3.
Now look at what the two share: two 2s and one 3.
Same answer as the lists, 12 — which is the check. For big numbers, the factor tree is usually the faster road.

youDo.title: Your turn — now a multiples question
lines: Ayasha has painting class every 8 weeks and pottery class every 6 weeks. Both are this week. When will both fall in the same week again?
List multiples of 8: 8, 16, 24, 32 … and multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24 …
Find the smallest number in both lists — that is the LCM.
Say what the LCM means for Ayasha, and explain why 48 is a common multiple but not the answer.

optional.stem: Is 4 a factor or a multiple of 12?
optional.explanation: 4 divides 12 evenly (12 ÷ 4 = 3), so 4 is a factor of 12. Multiples of 12 start at 12 and grow.
choiceFeedback: Multiples of 12 are 12, 24, 36 … — all at least 12.
4 divides 12, but 12 does not divide 4.
4 × 3 = 12, so it is definitely a factor.
hints: Does 4 divide 12 evenly?
Factors are at or below the number.
12 ÷ 4 = 3, no remainder.

optional.stem: What is the GCF of 10 and 15?
optional.explanation: Factors of 10: 1, 2, 5, 10. Factors of 15: 1, 3, 5, 15. They share 1 and 5; the greatest is 5.
choiceFeedback: 1 is common, but 5 is common and larger.
30 is a common multiple, not a factor.
10 does not divide 15 evenly.
hints: List the factors of each.
Which numbers are in both lists?
Take the largest one.

optional.stem: Match each pair to its greatest common factor.
optional.explanation: When two numbers share no factor except 1, their GCF is 1 — which is a real answer, not a mistake.
hints: List factors for each pair.
Look for the largest number in both lists.
7 and 9 share only 1.

optional.stem: Sort each statement about factors and multiples.

cards.text: There is a limited number of them

optional.explanation: Factors are finite and sit at or below the number; multiples are infinite and sit at or above it. Knowing this checks your answer before you write it down.
hints: Can you list every factor of 12? Every multiple?
Which grows without stopping?
Dividing versus skip-counting.

optional.title: Find the error
optional.correctWork: Step 2 drops 1 and 16. Every factor pair contributes both of its numbers, so the full list is 1, 2, 4, 8, 16.
optional.explanation: 1 and the number itself are always factors. Leaving them out is what makes a GCF come out too small.
hints: Look at the first factor pair in Step 1.
Does 1 divide 16 evenly? Does 16?
Include both numbers from every pair.

approaching.stem: Which list shows all the factors of 12?
approaching.explanation: A factor divides 12 evenly. Every one of 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, and 12 does, and nothing else does.
choiceFeedback: Those are MULTIPLES of 12 — where you land skip-counting, not what divides it.
1 and 12 are factors, but so are 2, 3, 4, and 6.
This list forgets 1 and 12, which are always factors of 12.
hints: Ask: what divides 12 with nothing left over?
Try each number from 1 up to 12.
Do not forget 1 and the number itself.

approaching.stem: Which list shows the first four multiples of 8?
approaching.explanation: Multiples come from multiplying by 1, 2, 3, 4: 8, 16, 24, and 32 — the numbers you say skip-counting by 8.
choiceFeedback: Those are the FACTORS of 8 — what divides it, not what it makes.
That counts up by 1, not by 8.
That counts by 2.
hints: Skip-count by 8 out loud.
Multiples get bigger; factors stay at or below the number.

approaching.stem: What is the greatest common factor of 12 and 18?
approaching.explanation: Factors of 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. Factors of 18: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18. They share 1, 2, 3, and 6 — the greatest is 6.
choiceFeedback: 3 is a common factor, but 6 is also common and larger.
36 is a common MULTIPLE, not a factor — a factor cannot be bigger than the numbers.
2 is a common factor, but not the greatest one.
hints: List the factors of each number.
Circle the numbers that appear in both lists.
Pick the largest circled number.

approaching.stem: Sort each number by its relationship to 10.
approaching.explanation: Factors divide 10 evenly and are never larger than 10. Multiples are what 10 builds and are never smaller than 10. The number 10 is both a factor and a multiple of itself.
hints: Ask: does this number divide 10, or does 10 divide it?
Factors are at or below 10.
Multiples are at or above 10.

approaching.stem: What is the least common multiple of 4 and 6?
approaching.explanation: Multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12 …; multiples of 6: 6, 12 …. The smallest they share is 12.
choiceFeedback: 24 is a common multiple, but 12 is smaller and also common.
2 is the greatest common FACTOR of 4 and 6, not a multiple.
10 is 4 + 6 — an LCM is not found by adding.
hints: List multiples of each number.
Look for the first number that appears in both lists.

approaching.title: Find the error

workedExample.label: Step 3
workedExample.work: The GCF is 36, because 36 is in both times tables.
workedExample.workEs: El MCD es 36, porque 36 está en las dos tablas de multiplicar.

approaching.correctWork: Step 3 names a common MULTIPLE, not a common factor. The common factors are 1, 2, 3, and 6, so the GCF is 6.
approaching.explanation: A factor can never be larger than the number it divides. Any answer bigger than 12 or 18 must be a multiple, which is the fastest way to catch this swap.
hints: Compare Step 3's answer to the two numbers themselves.
Can a factor of 12 be bigger than 12?
Look back at the numbers in BOTH lists.

onLevel.instructions: The store has 48 pencils and 36 notebooks. Complete the factor lists, then find the GCF.
onLevel.hint: List the factors of 36 in order, then compare the two lists.
hints: Work up from 1: does it divide 36 evenly?
The greatest number in both lists is the GCF.

onLevel.stem: Using prime factors, 48 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 and 36 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3. What is their GCF?
onLevel.explanation: Take only the primes both numbers have: two 2s and one 3. Multiplying them gives 2 × 2 × 3 = 12, matching the answer from the factor lists.
choiceFeedback: Multiplying every prime from both trees gives a common multiple, not a common factor.
Both numbers have TWO 2s in common, not one — so the 6 is short a factor of 2.
2 is shared, but 48 and 36 each contain two 2s and a 3, so more is shared than that.
hints: Circle the primes that appear in BOTH trees.
48 has four 2s and one 3; 36 has two 2s and two 3s.
Take the smaller count of each shared prime, then multiply.

onLevel.stem: Ayasha has painting every 8 weeks and pottery every 6 weeks, both this week. When do they next fall in the same week?
onLevel.explanation: Multiples of 8: 8, 16, 24 …; multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24 …. The first week they share is week 24.
choiceFeedback: 48 IS a common multiple, but the question asks for the first time they meet — 24 comes sooner.
14 is 8 + 6. Adding the cycles does not find when they line up.
2 is the GCF of 6 and 8 — a factor question, not a cycle question.
hints: List the weeks each class lands on.
Find the first week that appears in both lists.

onLevel.explanation: Splitting an existing amount into equal groups is a factor question; waiting for repeating cycles to line up is a multiple question. The size of the answer is a useful check on which one you used.
hints: Is the problem breaking something apart or counting forward?
Breaking apart → factors.
Counting forward in cycles → multiples.

onLevel.title: Find the error

workedExample.label: Problem
workedExample.work: Ayasha has painting every 8 weeks and pottery every 6 weeks. When do both fall in the same week?
workedExample.workEs: Ayasha tiene pintura cada 8 semanas y cerámica cada 6 semanas. ¿Cuándo caen ambas en la misma semana?

workedExample.label: Step 3
workedExample.work: The greatest common factor is 2, so both classes meet in week 2.
workedExample.workEs: El máximo común divisor es 2, así que ambas clases coinciden en la semana 2.

onLevel.correctWork: Step 1 starts down the wrong road: the classes REPEAT, so the weeks they land on are multiples, not factors. List multiples of 8 (8, 16, 24 …) and of 6 (6, 12, 18, 24 …); the first shared week is 24.
onLevel.explanation: The answer is also unreasonable on its face: a class that meets every 8 weeks cannot possibly happen in week 2. Checking the answer against the story catches the wrong tool immediately.
hints: Does a class every 8 weeks happen in week 2?
Are the weeks they meet factors of 8, or multiples of 8?
List the multiples of each and find the first shared one.

extending.title: Find the error

workedExample.label: Step 3
workedExample.work: Both lists contain 48, so the LCM is 48.
workedExample.workEs: Las dos listas contienen 48, así que el mcm es 48.

extending.correctWork: Step 3 picks a common multiple, but not the LEAST one. Both lists also contain 24, and 24 comes first — so the LCM is 24. (48 is the product 6 × 8, which is always A common multiple, just rarely the smallest.)
extending.explanation: Two numbers have infinitely many common multiples. The word LEAST is doing real work in the name, and scanning the lists from the start rather than the end is what finds it.
hints: Read both lists from the beginning, not the end.
Is there a smaller number in both lists than 48?
24 appears in both.

extending.stem: Reginald is having hot dogs for 24 guests and wants the same number of hot dogs and buns, with none left over. Hot dogs come in packs of 10 and buns in packs of 8. How many packs of each should he buy, and how many will he have? Explain which tool you used and why.
extending.sampleAnswer: This is a least-common-multiple problem: the pack sizes repeat, and he needs the first count both can reach exactly. Multiples of 10: 10, 20, 30, 40 …; multiples of 8: 8, 16, 24, 32, 40 …. The first number in both lists is 40, so the LCM of 10 and 8 is 40. That means 4 packs of hot dogs (4 × 10 = 40) and 5 packs of buns (5 × 8 = 40), giving 40 of each with nothing left over. It is a multiple problem rather than a factor one because nothing is being split into groups — he is counting packs forward until the two totals match. He will have 40 of each for 24 guests, which is more than enough; buying fewer packs would leave hot dogs or buns unmatched.
hints: Is he splitting an amount into groups, or counting packs forward until they match?
List the multiples of 10 and the multiples of 8.
Find the first total that both pack sizes can reach exactly.

practice.commonMistake: A common mistake is reaching for the wrong tool: listing FACTORS for a problem about repeating cycles. Ayasha's classes repeat every 6 and 8 weeks, so the weeks they land on are multiples — answering with the GCF of 2 claims a class that meets every 8 weeks happens in week 2. Use the size of the answer as a check: a GCF is never larger than the smaller number, and an LCM is never smaller than the larger one.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a prime number?
questions.explanation: 17 has exactly two factors: 1 and 17. 15 = 3 × 5, 21 = 3 × 7, and 9 = 3 × 3, so they are all composite.

questions.stem: What is the prime factorization of 18?
questions.explanation: 18 = 2 × 9 = 2 × 3 × 3. Both 2 and 3 are prime, so 2 × 3 × 3 is the prime factorization.

questions.stem: What is the prime factorization of 30?
questions.explanation: 30 = 2 × 15 = 2 × 3 × 5. All three factors (2, 3, 5) are prime, so 2 × 3 × 5 is the prime factorization.
